 Common Order
Since the issues involved in the petitions are interlinked, they are taken up together and a common order is being passed.
2. These petitions have been filed to recall the order passed by this Court in W.P.Nos.16445, 16447 and 16440 of 2025 dated 30.04.2025.

The petitioners have filed the Writ Petitions for a direction directing the respondents to de-freeze the accounts, which were already frozen by the respondents in pursuance to the registration of FIR in Crime No.1 of 2025 for offence punishable under Sections 406, 420, 120B, 109, 468, 506(1) of IPC.
Since the investigation was pending and procedure followed by the respondents was as contemplated under Section 102 of Cr.P.C., this Court dismissed the Writ Petitions.
As against the same, the petitioner has come up with these petitions to recall the said order.

The learned counsel for the petitioners would submit that after the dismissal of the writ petitions,
the petitioners filed copy application, seeking copy of the intimation letter sent by the 1st respondent to the learned Magistrate informing the freezing of bank accounts of the petitioners.
It was returned on the ground that no such intimation was filed before the learned Magistrate Court.

The learned counsel further submitted that in the delay application, this Court directed the 1st respondent to file an affidavit and in the said affidavit, the 1st respondent categorically had stated that for the seizure of the bank account Form 91 before the learned Magistrate was filed by the 1st respondent and the same was a false affidavit and as such, the order was passed without sending proper intimation as contemplated under Section 102(3) of Cr.P.C., and therefore the 1st respondent misrepresented before this Court.
Therefore, the order passed by this Court is liable to be recalled.

4. Per contra, the learned Government Advocate appearing for the 1st respondent submitted that in pursuance to the registration of FIR, accounts of the petitioners have been frozen for investigation purpose on 18.03.2025 and thereafter on 22.04.2025.

The intimation was duly sent to the learned Judicial Magistrate No.II, Salem, thereby intimating about https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis (

The 1st respondent had also produced the said intimation before the learned Magistrate by way of Form 91.

sentences.text: Heard the learned counsel on either side and perused the documents placed on record.

6. Originally, the petitioner filed petitions to de-freeze their accounts, which was frozen by the 1st respondent in pursuant to the registration of FIR in Crime No.1 of 2025 for offences under Sections 406, 420, 120B, 109, 468 506(1) IPC.

All the three Writ petitions were dismissed by this Court, as devoid of merits by considering the submissions made by the learned Public Prosecutor that Section 102(3) of Cr.P.C., procedure was duly complied with and the investigation was https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis ( Uploaded on: 20/08/2025 02:35:49 pm ) W.P.M.P.Crl.Nos.134 to 136 of 2025 also pending.

Now, the only contention raised by the learned counsel appearing for the petitioners is that the petitioners filed a copy application seeking a copy of intimation letter issued by the 1st respondent informing freezing of the bank account of the petitioners to the learned Judicial Magistrate No.II, Salem.
However, it was returned for the reason that no such document was filed by the 1st respondent.

7. On a perusal of the intimation letter produced before this Court dated 22.04.2025, it is revealed that it is in compliance with Section 102(3) of Cr.P.C, however, it does not form part of court records.

The seizure of accounts is equals to seizure of property under Form 91 and it was duly filed before the learned Judicial Magistrate No.II, Salem thereby informing the freezing of the accounts of the petitioners.
The form 91 shall form part of the court records, therefore, the petitioner is entitled for any record,which is part of it.

However, a perusal of the copy application filed by the petitioner reveals that petitioners sought for an intimation, which was sent by the 1st respondent about freezing of their accounts, however, it does not form part of the record, therefore, no party is entitled for the certified copy of the documents, which does not form part of the records.

Hence the learned Magistrate, rightly returned the https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis ( Uploaded on: 20/08/2025 02:35:49 pm ) W.P.M.P.Crl.Nos.134 to 136 of 2025 copy application, as no document was filed by the 1st respondent.

However, the Hon'ble Supreme court in a case Manu SC 0423 /2024 in Shento Varghese vs Julfikar Husen & others held as follows:-
17.

sentences.text: In the background of the aforesaid discussion, therefore, the line of precedents which have taken the position that seizure orders are vitiated for delay in compliance with the reporting obligation are declared to be manifestly erroneous and are accordingly, overruled.
The relevant question to be determined was not whether the duty of the police to report the seizure to the Magistrate is mandatory or directory.

Instead, what ought to have been inquired into was whether the exercise of the seizure power was subjected to compliance of reporting obligation, as illustrated in Section 105E Cr.P.C.
18.

Merely because we have held that non reporting of the seizure forthwith by the police officer to the jurisdictional court would not vitiate the seizure order, it would not mean that there would be no consequence whatsoever as regards the police Everest Blue Metals vs The State Rep.

3 officer, upon whom the law has enjoined a duty to act in a certain way.
Since there is an obligation cast on the officer to report the seizure forthwith, it becomes necessary to understand the meaning of the expression forthwith as used in Section 102(3) CrPC.
For, without a clear understanding of the said expression, the Magistrate would not be in a position to determine whether the obligation cast on the police officer has been properly complied with.

In this background, the expression shall forthwith report the seizure to the Magistrate https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis ( Uploaded on: 20/08/2025 02:35:49 pm ) W.P.M.P.Crl.Nos.134 to 136 of 2025 occurring in sub- section (3) of the Section 102 requires to be examined.

21. The expression forthwith has been defined in Blacks Law Dictionary, 10th Edition as under:
forthwith, adv. (14c) 1. Immediately; without delay.

2. Directly; promptly; within a reasonable time under the circumstances; with all convenient dispatch Whartons Law Lexicon, 17th Edition describes forthwith as extracted:
Forthwith, When a defendant is ordered to plead forthwith, he must plead within twenty four hours.

When a statute or rule of Court requires an act to be done forthwith, it means that the act is to be done within a reasonable time having regard to the object of the provision and the circumstances of the case [Ex parte Lamb,
(1881) 19 Ch D 169; 2 Chit. Arch. Prac., 14th Edition]
22.

From the discussion made above, it would emerge that the expression forthwith means as soon as may be, with reasonable speed and expedition, with a sense of urgency, and without any unnecessary delay.
In other words, it would mean as soon as possible, judged in the context of the object sought to be achieved or accomplished.

23. We are of the considered view that the said expression must receive a reasonable construction and in giving such construction, regard must be had to the nature of the act or thing to be performed and the prevailing circumstances of the case.

When it https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis ( Uploaded on: 20/08/2025 02:35:49 pm ) W.P.M.P.Crl.Nos.134 to 136 of 2025 is not the mandate of the law that the act should be done within a fixed time, it would mean that the act must be done within a reasonable time.
It all depends upon the circumstances that may unfold in a given case and there cannot be a straight-jacket formula prescribed in this regard.
In that sense, the interpretation of the word forthwith would depend upon the terrain in which it travels and would take its colour depending upon the prevailing circumstances which can be variable.

24. Therefore, in deciding whether the police officer has properly discharged his obligation under Section 102(3) Cr.P.C., the Magistrate would have to, firstly, examine whether the seizure was reported forthwith.

In doing so, it ought to have regard to the interpretation of the expression,
forthwith as discussed above.
If it finds that the report was not sent forthwith, then it must examine whether there is any explanation offered in support of the delay.
If the Magistrate finds that the delay has been properly explained, it would leave the matter at that.
However, if it finds that there is no reasonable explanation for the delay or that the official has acted with deliberate Everest Blue Metals vs The State Rep.

Thus it is clear that the expression forthwith means as soon as may be, with reasonable speed and expedition, with a sense of urgency, and without any unnecessary delay.

In the case on hand,
the 1st respondent had frozen the account of the petitioners on 18.03.2025 and the same was intimated to the learned Magistrate on 22.04.2025.
Though there was a delay in intimation, it was within a reasonable time, depends upon the allegation levelled against the petitioners.

Further,
eventhough there was a delay in intimating about freezing of accounts, it was not mandated by law that the act should be done within a fixed time, it is rather stated that the act should be done within a reasonable time and further, there cannot be any straight-jacket formula prescribed in this regard,
therefore, even the said delay would not vitiate seizure of the accounts, therefore, this Court does not find any reason to recall the order passed by this Court.
9.
